Commentary of al-Sam'ani (Tafsir al-Quran) on surah 36, verse 1:

In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful.

Tafsir of Surat Ya-Sin

It is a Meccan surah. Muqatil ibn Hayyan narrated from Qatadah, from Anas, from the Prophet (ﷺ), who said: "Indeed, everything has a heart, and the heart of the Qur'an is Surat Ya-Sin. Whoever recites Surat Ya-Sin, Allah will grant him the reward of reciting the Qur'an ten times."

This report is gharib (rare, with a weak chain). Abu 'Isa (al-Tirmidhi) included it in his Jami', and Allah knows best.

Allah's words: ﴿Ya-Sin﴾. Ibn 'Abbas said: it is an oath that Allah swore by. Qatadah said: it is a name of the surah. Mujahid said: Ya-Sin is among the opening letters of the Qur'an. Al-Hasan, Sa'id ibn Jubayr, al-Dahhak and a group said that the meaning of His words ﴿Ya-Sin﴾ is "O man," and this is the most well-known of the opinions. Tha'lab said: it is "O man" in the dialect of Tayy. Another said: in the dialect of Kalb. 'Isa ibn 'Umar read it as "Yasin" with a fatha, and it is said that its meaning is: "O Muhammad."

His words: ﴿And the wise Qur'an﴾, meaning: and the Qur'an which is perfected (ahkama) with commands, prohibitions, reward and punishment,

And His saying, ﴿Indeed, you are among the messengers﴾. On this basis the oath was made; it is as if God, exalted is He, swore by the Qur'an that Muhammad is among the messengers.

It is narrated from ʿAlī, may Allah be pleased with him, that he said: Allah named His Messenger Muhammad in
The Qur'an [has] seven names: Muhammad, Ahmad, Taha, Yasin, al-Muddaththir, al-Muzzammil, and Abdullah.

Regarding His words ﴿on a straight path﴾, there are two possibilities. The first: it is a predicate following another predicate. The second: its meaning is, "Indeed you are among the messengers who are upon a straight path."

"And His saying: ﴿A revelation from the Mighty, the Merciful﴾ — meaning: it is a revelation from the Mighty, the Merciful. It was also read as "tanzīl" with a fatḥah on the lām, meaning: Allah sent it down as a revelation from the Mighty, the Merciful."

On the words of Allah, the Exalted: ﴿So that you may warn a people whose fathers were not warned, so they are heedless﴾. Regarding this there are two opinions. The first: that "mā" (مَا) is negative, and the meaning is: their fathers were not warned at all, for Allah, the Exalted, sent none to the Quraysh other than the Prophet.

The second opinion: that "mā" here means "alladhī" (the one which), so the meaning of the verse according to this is: so that you may warn a people with that which their fathers were warned with.

As for His words: ﴿so they are heedless﴾, i.e., of the warning. Al-Naqqash related in his tafsir, from the Prophet (ﷺ), that Mudar had embraced Islam.

Abu 'Ubayda related that Tamim used to be called Abu Zayd, and he had an idol that he worshipped. Then he embraced Islam and buried his idol. Then his son Zayd dug the idol out from that place and worshipped it, so Zayd was named Manat.

The Almighty's saying: ﴿Certainly the word has come into effect﴾, meaning: the word has become binding upon most of them. The meaning of the word becoming binding is the binding of the judgment of punishment. And His saying: ﴿[upon most of them], so they do not believe﴾, meaning: they do not affirm.

Commentary of al-Sam'ani (Tafsir al-Quran) on surah 36, verse 8:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Indeed, We have put on their necks shackles﴾. If it is said: the shackle (ghull) is only placed on the hand! The answer to this is: the custom is that the hand is shackled up to the neck, so He mentioned the necks for this meaning, and sufficed by mentioning them over mentioning the hands. Al-Azhari said: the meaning of the verse is: "Indeed, We have put shackles on their necks and their hands," so it is a metonymy (kinayah) for the hands.

If it is said: how can one refer metonymically to the hands when they have not been mentioned? The answer to this is: the Arabs refer metonymically to a thing even when it has not been mentioned, if it is known.

The poet said:

(And I do not know, when I set out for a land, seeking good, which of them will come near me:)
(Is it the good that I am seeking, or the evil that is seeking me?)

So by his saying "which of them" he referred metonymically to the evil and the good, though the evil was not mentioned.

His saying: ﴿up to the chins﴾ means: up to the necks, except that He mentioned the chins because the necks are close to the chins. His saying: ﴿so they are raised-heads﴾. The muqmah is the one who raises his head and lowers his gaze. The Arabs call the two Kanun (the months of December and January) the two months of qimah, because camels drink water and raise their heads from the intensity of the cold. The poet said:

(And we, sitting on its sides, lowering our gaze like camels with raised heads.)

Ibn Mas'ud recited: "Indeed, We have put shackles on their right hands," and this reading is well known from him.

The words of the Most High: ﴿And We have placed a barrier before them﴾. It is also read as "sadan" (سدا) with a *ḍamma* on the *sīn* (سُدا).

ʿIkrimah said: Whatever is made by God is a *sadd* (barrier), and whatever is made by created beings is also a *sadd*. Others said: the *sadd* is what can be seen, and the *sadd* is also what cannot be seen. Some did not distinguish between the two and said they have the same meaning.

The exegetes (*ahl al-tafsīr*, the people of tafsir, i.e. Qur'anic exegesis) said: The mention of the barrier here is by way of a parable. Likewise, the mention of the shackles in the first verse, according to some of them, is also a parable, and the meaning of the shackles is that they are prevented from spending in the way of God. The meaning of the barrier is that they are prevented from guidance. Some of them mentioned that the verse was revealed on a specific occasion: a group of the Banu Makhzum conferred about killing the Prophet (ﷺ). One of them came to kill him while he was praying, but he could hear his voice and could not see his person. Another came and saw a great thing intending to destroy him, so he feared and turned back. It is said that the second was Abu Jahl, may the curse of God be upon him. God, exalted is He, then revealed this verse concerning this, which is His saying: ﴿And We have placed a barrier before them﴾.

His saying: ﴿So We covered them﴾ comes from *taghshiyah* (covering) and *taghṭiyah* (concealing). Ibn ʿAbbas and ʿUmar ibn ʿAbd al-ʿAzīz read "fa-aghshaynāhum" (فأغشيناهم) with an unpointed ʿayn (غ... "fa-aʿshaynāhum", i.e. with the letter ʿayn without dots), from His saying: ﴿And whoever turns away from the remembrance of the Most Merciful, We appoint for him a devil who becomes his companion [so he is his companion]﴾, meaning he becomes blind. So the meaning of His saying ﴿We covered them﴾ is: We made them blind.

His saying: ﴿So they do not see﴾ means: the path of truth.

"His saying, exalted is He: ﴿It is the same for them whether you warn them or do not warn them; they will not believe﴾. This refers to specific people, who have passed away without believing, as Allah, exalted is He, said."

Commentary of al-Sam'ani (Tafsir al-Quran) on surah 36, verse 11:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Verily you can only warn one who follows the Reminder and fears the Most Merciful unseen.﴾ That is: one who listens to the Reminder, which is the Qur'an, and follows what is in it. And His saying: ﴿and fears the Most Merciful unseen﴾ means: he fears the Most Merciful in the unseen.

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿So give him the good news of forgiveness and a noble reward.﴾ That is: Paradise.

Commentary of al-Sam'ani (Tafsir al-Quran) on surah 36, verse 12:

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Indeed, it is We who bring the dead to life﴾, meaning: on the Day of Resurrection. It is also said: He gives life to dead hearts with the light of faith. And His saying: ﴿and We record what they have put forward﴾, meaning: what they have hastened (ahead).

And His saying: ﴿and their traces﴾, meaning: and We record their traces. Regarding "their traces" there are two opinions. The first: that its meaning is what they established of a good or evil practice (sunnah).

The second opinion: that His saying ﴿and their traces﴾ means the steps taken toward the mosques. Abu Sa'id al-Khudri narrated: "The dwellings of the Banu Salamah were in a remote part of the mosque's vicinity, so they wanted to move closer to the mosque. The Prophet said to them: 'Your dwellings, your dwellings, your traces are recorded,' so they abandoned the move."

It has also been related in a report from the Prophet (ﷺ) that he said: "Whoever establishes a good practice will have its reward and the reward of whoever acts upon it until the Day of Resurrection, without any diminishing of their rewards; and whoever establishes a bad practice will bear its burden and the burden of whoever acts upon it until the Day of Resurrection, without any diminishing of their burdens."

And His saying: ﴿and We have enumerated everything in a clear Imam﴾, meaning: We have gathered it in a clear Book, and the clear Imam is the Preserved Tablet (al-Lawh al-Mahfuz).

The Qur'anic phrase in verse 13 of surah Ya-Sin is ﴿وَاضْرِبْ لَهُم مثلا﴾, which I translate as: ﴿And present to them an example﴾.

Commentary of al-Sam'ani (Tafsir al-Quran) on surah 36, verse 13:

His statement, the Exalted: ﴿And present to them an example﴾. Ḍarb al-mathal (striking an example, i.e. presenting a parable) is tamthīl al-mathal (depicting a parable), and the meaning of the verse is: "Recount to them the example of their situation from the story of the people of the town."

As for the town (al-qaryah): most of the exegetes say that the town is Antioch (Anṭākiyyah). Some of them said: it is a city from the lands of the Romans. His statement: ﴿when the messengers came to them﴾ — in the narrative: ʿĪsā (ʿalayhi al-salām) sent to them two men from the Ḥawāriyyūn (the disciples), then sent a third after them. This is the meaning of His statement, the Exalted:

Commentary of al-Sam'ani (Tafsir al-Quran) on surah 36, verse 14:

﴿When We sent to them two messengers, and they denied them both, We reinforced them with a third.﴾ The third one, whose name was Shamʿun (Simon), the head of the disciples (al-Hawariyyun), and His saying: ﴿reinforced⁠﴾ means: We strengthened and fortified. ʿAsim alone recited "fa-ʿazzaznā" with a light (single-z) pronunciation, and it has the same meaning as the first.

In the exegesis: the people denied the first two messengers and intended to kill them. Then this third one came and gently gained entry to the king. His daughter had died and been buried. He said to the king: "Ask these two men to revive your daughter; if they revive her, then they are truthful." So the king asked them to do so. They both stood up, prayed, and called upon Allah the Exalted, and Shamʿun prayed along with them in secret. Allah the Exalted revived the woman, the grave split open over her, and she came out. She said to the people: "Submit, for they are truthful, and I do not think you will submit." Then she asked the two messengers to return her to her place, so they cast dust upon her head, and she returned to her grave as she had been. And the people did not believe.
The words of Allah, the Exalted: ﴿They said, "You are but human beings like us, and the Most Merciful has sent down nothing. You are only lying."﴾ Its apparent meaning is clear.

Commentary of al-Sam'ani (Tafsir al-Quran) on surah 36, verse 16:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿They said: Our Lord knows that we are indeed sent to you﴾. If it is said: How can God's knowledge that they are messengers of God be a proof against them?

The answer to this: its meaning is: "Our Lord knows that we are indeed sent to you, by means of the signs and miracles He manifested at our hands. Thus the proof was established by the signs and miracles, not by the mere fact of knowledge."
And His saying: ﴿And upon us is only the clear conveyance﴾, meaning: the plain conveyance (of the message).

Commentary of al-Sam'ani (Tafsir al-Quran) on surah 36, verse 18:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿They said, "Indeed, we consider you a bad omen (tatayyarna) for us"﴾. That is: we consider you an ill omen (tashá'amna bikum). It is mentioned in the tafsir that the rain had been withheld from them when these messengers came to them.

Scholars differed over whether they were messengers of God or messengers of Jesus. One of the two opinions is that they were messengers of Jesus, peace be upon him, as we have explained. The other opinion is that they were messengers of God.

His saying: ﴿"If you do not desist, we will surely stone you"﴾. That is: [we will kill you] by stoning. It was also said: we will revile you. The first is more preferable.

His saying: ﴿"And a painful punishment from us will surely touch you"﴾. That is: painful (mu'lim), and the painful is the one who causes pain (al-muwji').

"The Most High said: ﴿They said: Your omen is with yourselves.﴾ That is: your ill omen is with you, through your disbelief and your denial of the messengers.

It was also said: "Your omen is with yourselves" means: your fates and your deeds follow you. The Arabs say: "ṭāra" in the sense of "ṣāra" (became). The poet said:

(The forelocks of polytheism fly, both the even and the odd, and leadership belongs to the boy.)

It was also said: "Your omen is with yourselves" means: whatever good or evil has flown to you [as your lot] is with you and clings to you. As for His words: ﴿Is it because you were reminded?﴾, its meaning: is it because you were reminded of God that you took omens? It is also read "an dhakartum" (because you were reminded), meaning: because you were reminded, you took omens. As for His words: ﴿Nay, you are a people who exceed the limit﴾, that is: those who transgress the bounds."

Commentary of al-Sam'ani (Tafsir al-Quran) on surah 36, verse 20:

The words of Allah the Exalted: ﴿And there came from the farthest part of the city a man running﴾. Most of the exegetes held that he was a man called Habib al-Najjar (Habib the carpenter). Al-Suddi said: he was a cloth-beater (qassar). It is also reported from some of them that he was a cobbler (iskafa). Qatadah said: he was a man who worshipped Allah in a cave; he heard the news of the messengers, so he came to them and said: "Do you ask for any payment for your message?" They said: "No." Then he turned to his people and said to them what Allah has related, and this is His saying: ﴿O my people, follow the messengers﴾. The "madina" (city) is the town we have mentioned, and it is Antioch (al-Antakiya).

The Qur'anic verse is: ﴿Follow those who ask you no reward, and who are guided.﴾ Its meaning is evident.

It is related from some of them that he said: "The dwelling of the nobles is at the edges," and he cited as evidence this verse, namely His saying: ﴿And there came from the farthest part of the city a man running﴾ — that is, from the most distant place in the city.

Commentary of al-Sam'ani (Tafsir al-Quran) on surah 36, verse 22:

The words of the Most High: ﴿And why should I not worship He who originated me?﴾ mean: And why should I not worship He who originated me? ﴿And to Him you will be returned.﴾

If it is said: How did he attribute the origination (fitrah) to himself while attributing the return to them?

The answer to this is: He attributed the origination to himself because the blessing upon him was more manifest, and he attributed the return to them because the admonition (zajr) was more fitting for them, and in mentioning the return there is the meaning of admonition.

The Almighty's words: ﴿Shall I take besides Him gods?﴾ is a interrogative in the sense of denial, meaning: I shall not take them. His words: ﴿If the Most Merciful intends for me some harm﴾ means: some evil and adversity. His words: ﴿Their intercession will avail me nothing﴾ mean: the idols will not avail me anything, because they have no intercession, although the disbelievers used to claim that they would intercede for them on the Day of Resurrection.

And His words: ﴿nor can they save me﴾ mean: they cannot save me from the punishment if God were to punish me.
"His saying: ﴿Indeed, I would then be in clear error﴾ — meaning: I would be in manifest mistake if I did this."
Allah's words: ﴿Indeed, I have believed in your Lord, so listen to me.﴾ Abu 'Ubayda said: its majaz (figurative sense) is "so listen to me."

Commentary of al-Sam'ani (Tafsir al-Quran) on surah 36, verses 26–27:

His saying: ﴿It was said: Enter Paradise﴾. In the tafsir: when he said this statement, the people rushed upon him in a single rush and trampled him with their feet until they killed him. This is related from Ibn Mas'ud. It is also said: they trampled him until his intestine (qasab) came out through his anus. So God admitted him into Paradise, and he is there alive, being provided for. This is the meaning of His saying: ﴿It was said: Enter Paradise﴾.

And His saying: ﴿Would that my people knew of how my Lord has forgiven me﴾, meaning: of the forgiveness of my Lord toward me. Qatadah said: "He advised them while alive and after death." And His saying: ﴿and made me among the honored﴾, meaning: among those who entered Paradise. Whoever is admitted into Paradise has been honored, and whoever is admitted into the Fire has been humiliated.

Commentary of al-Sam'ani (Tafsir al-Quran) on surah 36, verses 26–27:

His saying: ﴿It was said: Enter Paradise﴾. In the tafsir: when he said this statement, the people rushed upon him in a single rush and trampled him with their feet until they killed him. This is related from Ibn Mas'ud. It is also said: they trampled him until his intestine (qasab) came out through his anus. So God admitted him into Paradise, and he is there alive, being provided for. This is the meaning of His saying: ﴿It was said: Enter Paradise﴾.

And His saying: ﴿Would that my people knew of how my Lord has forgiven me﴾, meaning: of the forgiveness of my Lord toward me. Qatadah said: "He advised them while alive and after death." And His saying: ﴿and made me among the honored﴾, meaning: among those who entered Paradise. Whoever is admitted into Paradise has been honored, and whoever is admitted into the Fire has been humiliated.

Almost none of the passage contains technical terms needing glosses beyond the Qur'anic quotations, which I translate plainly.

Commentary of al-Sam'ani (Tafsir al-Quran) on surah 36, verse 28:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And We did not send down upon his people after him any army from the heaven﴾, meaning: from angels. And His saying: ﴿And We were not going to send down﴾, meaning: We were not going to do this; rather, the matter of their destruction was easier than you suppose.

Commentary of al-Sam'ani (Tafsir al-Quran) on surah 36, verse 29:

The words of the Exalted: ﴿It was but a single shout﴾, meaning: it was not but a single shout.

In the narration concerning the story: Jibril, peace be upon him, came and stood at the gate of the city and cried out at them with a single cry, and they fell dead as if they had never been, and became like ashes, extinguished and still.

And in the reports: When 'Urwa ibn Mas'ud al-Thaqafi embraced Islam, he asked the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) for permission to go to his people, the Thaqif, and invite them to Islam. The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "I fear that they will kill you." He said: "Had I been asleep, they would not have awakened me." Then he went to them and invited them to Islam, and a man shot him with an arrow which struck his main artery (akhal), and he died. When the Prophet (ﷺ) learned of this, he said: "He is in this community like the companion of Ya-Sin, and he is Habib al-Najjar."

Commentary of al-Sam'ani (Tafsir al-Quran) on surah 36, verse 30:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Alas for the servants!﴾ If it is said: How is the address of "alas" (ḥasrah) consistent, since "alas" does not understand anything? And also, how does God, exalted is He, feel regret (yataḥassar) over the servants whom He destroyed, when this attribute is not permissible for Him? The answer to this: the meaning of the speaker's saying "yā ḥasrah" (alas!) is like his saying "yā ʿajaban" (how strange!). Likewise his saying "yā ḥasratā" is like his saying "yā ʿajabā". The Arabs say this by way of emphasis, and the address (nidāʾ) in their usage has the meaning of alerting (tanbīh). So it is consistent both with one who understands and with one who does not. And his saying "yā ʿajabā" is more emphatic than their saying "I am amazed at such-and-such", as if he said: "O wonder, this is your time! O regret, this is your era!" The true meaning is that this time is a time of regret and amazement.

As for his saying that regret upon God is not permissible: we say, yes. The meaning of the verse is: "Alas for the servants because of themselves"; it is as if they were regretting themselves to the utmost degree of regret. Ḥasrah (regret) is grief over a matter that has passed, in its most intense forms, until a man is left exhausted and cut off from his intensity. In the irregular reading (shādh) it is recited: "yā ḥasrata l-ʿibād" (Alas, the regret of the servants!). Another answer: He, exalted is He, said: ﴿Alas for the servants!﴾ because they have come to be in the position of those over whom one feels regret. It is also said that its meaning is: "Alas, the regret of the messengers and the angels over the servants." The first answer is the best of the answers.

His saying: ﴿There does not come to them any messenger except that they used to mock him﴾, i.e., the mockery of denial.

Commentary of al-Sam'ani (Tafsir al-Quran) on surah 36, verse 31:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Have they not seen how many generations We have destroyed before them?﴾ Ibn Mas'ud recited "Have they not seen whom We have destroyed" (man ahlakna), whereas the well-known reading is "how many" (kam ahlakna), and it is for multiplication (al-takthir).

And His saying: ﴿from the generations﴾ (al-qurun). The scholars differed concerning the duration of a generation (al-qarn), and we have explained this before. It has been narrated from the Prophet (ﷺ) that he said to Abdullah ibn Bisr al-Mazini: "You will live a generation (qarn)," and he lived a hundred years. And His saying: ﴿that they do not return to them﴾ means: they do not return to this world (al-dunya).

The words of the Most High: ﴿And all of them, [each] brought before Us﴾. Here "إن" (in) means "ما" (not), and "لما" (lamma) means "إلا" (except), so the meaning of the verse is: "And they are all none other than gathered and brought before Us." It is also in this reading in the Mushaf (the codex, the written copy of the Qur'an) of Ubayy ibn Ka'b.

Commentary of al-Sam'ani (Tafsir al-Quran) on surah 36, verse 33:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And a sign for them is the dead earth﴾. It is also read "al-maytah" with the doubled letter (tashdid).

And His saying: ﴿We have revived it﴾, i.e., with rain.

And His saying: ﴿and We bring forth from it grain﴾, i.e., wheat, barley, and the like. And His saying: ﴿so from it they eat﴾, i.e., from the grain they eat.

Commentary of al-Sam'ani (Tafsir al-Quran) on surah 36, verse 34–35:

The words of Allah the Exalted: ﴿And We placed therein gardens of palm trees and grapevines﴾, meaning: in the earth there are gardens of palm trees and grapevines.

And His words: ﴿and We caused springs to gush forth within them, that they might eat of its fruit﴾, meaning: and We caused water to gush forth within them from the springs, so that they might eat of the fruit produced by the water.

And His words: ﴿and that which their hands had made﴾, meaning: and that they might eat of what their hands had made, of that which they plough, sow and plant. It is also recited as "and what their hands made" (wa-ma 'amilat aydihim), with the same meaning as the first reading.

The second opinion regarding the verse is that "mā" (what) here is a negation (lā), and its meaning is: We provided for them with what their hands did not make.

And His words: ﴿Will they not then be thankful?﴾, meaning: for these blessings.

Commentary of al-Sam'ani (Tafsir al-Quran) on surah 36, verse 34–35:

The words of Allah the Exalted: ﴿And We placed therein gardens of palm trees and grapevines﴾, meaning: in the earth there are gardens of palm trees and grapevines.

And His words: ﴿and We caused springs to gush forth within them, that they might eat of its fruit﴾, meaning: and We caused water to gush forth within them from the springs, so that they might eat of the fruit produced by the water.

And His words: ﴿and that which their hands had made﴾, meaning: and that they might eat of what their hands had made, of that which they plough, sow and plant. It is also recited as "and what their hands made" (wa-ma 'amilat aydihim), with the same meaning as the first reading.

The second opinion regarding the verse is that "mā" (what) here is a negation (lā), and its meaning is: We provided for them with what their hands did not make.

And His words: ﴿Will they not then be thankful?﴾, meaning: for these blessings.

Commentary of al-Sam'ani (Tafsir al-Quran) on surah 36, verse 36:

The words of God, Exalted: ﴿Glory be to Him who created all the pairs﴾. That is: all the kinds.

And His words: ﴿Glory be to Him who﴾ means: glorify God, who created all the pairs. And His words: ﴿of what the earth produces, and of themselves, and of that which they do not know﴾ mean: of the plants, and the animals that they do not know.

Some of the exegetes mentioned that what they do not know here is the soul (rūḥ), and God created the soul within the self, and no one knows it. Others mentioned that His words ﴿and what their hands have made﴾ refer to the springs, and among the springs and rivers are those that human hands have not made, such as the Tigris (Dijla), the Euphrates (al-Furat), the Nile (al-Nil), Seyhan (Sīḥān), and Ceyhan (Jayḥān).

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And a sign for them is the night; We strip the day away from it, and then they are plunged into darkness﴾. "Naslakh" means: We scrape off and remove. Its meaning: We take away the day and bring in the night, as if the day were extracted from it. And His saying: ﴿then they are in darkness﴾ means: they enter into the darkness.

Commentary of al-Sam'ani (Tafsir al-Quran) on surah 36, verse 38:

The Almighty's saying: ﴿And the sun runs on to a resting place for it﴾. Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, recited: "And the sun runs on to a resting place for it" — meaning: it moves and runs always, without rest (qarar) and without stopping (wuquf). As for the well-known reading, "li-mustaqarr lahā" (to a resting place for it), there are two opinions on it.

The first: its resting place is the end of its circuit when the Hour is established.

The second opinion: its resting place is the end of its rising in the sky in summer, and the end of its descent in winter. And it has been related from the Prophet (ﷺ) through the transmission of al-A'mash, from Ibrahim al-Taymi, from his father, from Abu Dharr, that he said: "I was with the Prophet (ﷺ) until the sun set, and he said: 'O Abu Dharr, do you know where it goes?' I said: 'Allah and His Messenger know best.' He said: 'It goes and seeks permission to prostrate.'" And in another narration: "It goes beneath the Throne and seeks permission to prostrate; permission is granted to it to prostrate, and it is said to it: 'Rise from where you used to rise.' And it seems that one day it was said to it: 'O Abu Dharr, rise from where you came'; so it rises from its west." Then the Prophet (ﷺ) recited the Almighty's saying: ﴿And that is its resting place﴾. He said: "And in this report it is the same in the recitation of Abdullah ibn Mas'ud."

The Shaykh, the Imam, said: This report was related to us by Abd al-Rahman ibn Abd Allah ibn Ahmad, who said: Abu al-Abbas al-Tahhan related to us, who said: Abu al-Abbas ibn Mahbub related to us, who said: Abu Isa al-Tirmidhi related to us, who said: [Hannad ibn al-Sarri related to us, who said:] Abu Mu'awiya al-Darir related to us, from al-A'mash… the report.

As for His saying: ﴿That is the decree of the Almighty, the All-Knowing﴾, its meaning is clear. Al-Bukhari also mentioned in the Sahih, through the narration of Abu Dharr as well, that he asked the Prophet (ﷺ) about the Almighty's saying: ﴿And the sun runs on to a resting place for it﴾, and he said: "Its resting place is beneath the Throne."

Al-Azhari mentioned regarding His saying: ﴿runs on to a resting place for it﴾, that it means: it runs until the term that was appointed for it, and the measure that was decreed for it.

Commentary of al-Sam'ani (Tafsir al-Quran) on surah 36, verse 39:

His words, may He be exalted: ﴿And the moon — We have determined for it phases﴾. It is read with a nominative (raf') and it is read with an accusative (nasb). As for the accusative: "And We have determined the moon into phases." As for the nominative, its meaning is: "And a sign for them is the moon — We have determined it into phases."

It is narrated that Sa'id ibn al-Musayyab heard a man reciting poetry:

("The moon set, which I had hoped would set (in peace), / and the herdsmen's spirit, and the nightly chatter of the evening revelers.")

He said: "May Allah fight him! He has belittled what Allah has magnified. Allah the Exalted says: ﴿And the moon — We have determined for it phases﴾."

As for His words: ﴿until it becomes like the old dried palm-stalk (al-'urjun al-qadim)﴾. Ja'far ibn Muhammad said: "Like the stalk of an old palm-date cluster." Most scholars hold that the 'urjun is the stem of the bunch (kubbasa) when it is dried, withered and curved.

As for His words: ﴿al-qadim﴾, it means "the withered," and it is said that al-qadim is that which has passed over it a full year.

As for the phases (manazil) of the moon, they are twenty-eight phases: al-Saratan, al-Butayn, al-Thurayya, al-Dabaran, al-Haq'a, al-Han'a, al-Dhira', al-Nathra, al-Tarf, al-Jabha, al-Zubra, al-Sarfa, al-'Awwa', al-Simak, al-Ghafr, al-Zubana, al-Iklil, al-Qalb, al-Shawla, al-Na'a'im, al-Balda, Sa'd al-Dhabih, Sa'd Bula', Sa'd al-Su'ud, Sa'd al-Akhbiya, Fargh al-Dalw al-Muqaddam, Fargh al-Dalw al-Mu'akhkhar, and Batn al-Hut.

These are twenty-eight lunar mansions: the moon descends into one of them each night, and fourteen of them are always visible while fourteen of them are hidden; whenever one mansion rises, another sets. It is said: "The one that sets is the watcher of the one that rises." Twelve of them occur in the darkness of the night from the time of sunset until the time of dawn, and two of them from the rising of dawn until the rising of the sun.

Commentary of al-Sam'ani (Tafsir al-Quran) on surah 36, verse 40:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿It is not for the sun to overtake the moon﴾, meaning: the night does not enter upon the day before the day has finished, and the day does not enter upon the night before the night has finished.

His saying: ﴿nor does the night outstrip the day﴾, meaning: they alternate according to a known reckoning until the world comes to an end. And He says: ﴿It is not for the sun to overtake the moon﴾, meaning: the sun does not rise by night, and the moon does not rise by day, and the moon has its light, so neither of them enters into the domain of the other.

It is said: neither of them departs from the meaning of the other. Yahya ibn Sallam mentioned that the saying of He, may He be exalted, ﴿It is not for the sun to overtake the moon﴾ refers specifically to the night of the full moon, for the sun does not rise except after the moon has set, so the two do not meet in visible sight. It is also said: "it does not overtake it" means it does not join it in one orbit (falak), for they said: the sun is in the fourth heaven and the moon is in the lowest heaven.

His saying: ﴿nor does the night outstrip the day﴾, meaning: one night does not follow directly upon another night without a day separating them.

His saying: ﴿and each in an orbit they swim﴾, meaning: they run and revolve.

Commentary of al-Sam'ani (Tafsir al-Quran) on surah 36, verse 41:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And a sign for them is that We carried their offspring﴾, meaning: their forefathers. This is what Tha'lab and others said, and the word dhurriyyah (offspring), just as it applies to sons, also applies to fathers.

And His saying: ﴿in the laden ship﴾, meaning: the fully loaded. It was also said: the filled. It is reported from 'Ali ibn Abi Talib, may Allah be pleased with him, that he said: the intended meaning of the verse is that We carried them in the wombs of their mothers, and the wombs of the mothers were likened to laden ships.

Commentary of al-Sam'ani (Tafsir al-Quran) on surah 36, verse 42:

The words of Allah the Exalted: ﴿And We have created for them the like of it which they ride﴾ have two interpretations.

The first: what is meant is the small boats and the ships that sail on the rivers. They are, on the rivers, like the great ships on the sea. This is the view of Qatadah, al-Dahhak and others.

The second view, which is what Abu Salih narrated from Ibn 'Abbas: the meaning of His words ﴿And We have created for them the like of it which they ride﴾ is: the camels. Camels in the deserts are like ships on the seas.
Allah the Exalted says: ﴿And if We will, We drown them, and there is no one to cry out for them﴾. That is: there is no helper for them. ﴿Nor are they rescued﴾. That is: nor are they saved.

And His saying: ﴿Except as a mercy from Us﴾ means: their rescue is by Our mercy.

And His saying: ﴿and as enjoyment for a time﴾ means: that they may enjoy themselves until a known term.

Commentary of al-Sam'ani (Tafsir al-Quran) on surah 36, verse 45:

The words of Allah the Exalted: ﴿And when it is said to them, "Beware of what is before you and what is behind you"﴾, meaning: beware of what is before you, that is, the Resurrection, so be wary of it; ﴿and what is behind you﴾, meaning: this world, so do not be deceived by it.

The second opinion: the meaning of His words ﴿Beware of what is before you﴾ is: beware of the like of the punishment of the nations who were before you, lest there befall you the like of what befell them.

And His words ﴿and what is behind you﴾ mean: beware of the punishment of the Fire. And His words ﴿so that you may receive mercy﴾ mean: be people who hope for mercy.
Allah's words: ﴿And no sign from the signs of their Lord comes to them except that they turn away from it﴾. That is, turning away in denial and rejection.

Commentary of al-Sam'ani (Tafsir al-Quran) on surah 36, verse 47:

And His, the Exalted's, saying: ﴿And when it is said to them, "Spend from what Allah has provided you,"﴾ meaning: from what Allah has given you.

And His saying: ﴿Those who disbelieve say to those who believe, "Shall we feed those whom, if Allah willed, He would feed?"﴾

Ibn 'Abbas said: There were zindiqs (heretics; freethinkers who concealed unbelief) in Makkah, and when it was said to them, "Spend on the poor from what Allah has given you," they would say this statement mockingly. And from al-Basri he said: This is the saying of the Jews, who would say: "How can we give to them when Allah has impoverished them? And if He willed to give them, He would have given them?" And al-Qutaybi mentioned in his book al-Ma'arif that Abu al-Aswad al-Du'ali was among those whom He made wealthy from his creation. So this is the argument of the miserly in stinginess, and it is a false argument, because Allah, the Exalted, withheld worldly provision from the poor not out of stinginess but as a trial, and He commanded the wealthy to spend not because He had need of their wealth but as a trial of their gratitude.

And His saying: ﴿You are only in clear error.﴾ meaning: you are in manifest error.
Allah the Exalted says: ﴿And they say, "When is this promise, if you are truthful?"﴾ That is, the promise of the Resurrection.

Commentary of al-Sam'ani (Tafsir al-Quran) on surah 36, verse 49:

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿They await nothing but a single blast which will seize them while they are disputing﴾. That is: "yakhtasimun" (they dispute). So it is also in the recitation of Ubayy ibn Ka'b. It is said: "hum yakhsimun" means they bargain with one another over their needs. And in a report from the Prophet (ﷺ): "The Hour will come while a man is watering his livestock, and it will come while a man is smoothing his pool, and it will come while a man is displaying his goods for sale, and it will come while a man has raised his morsel to put it in his mouth, and it will come before he puts it into his mouth."

Commentary of al-Sam'ani (Tafsir al-Quran) on surah 36, verse 50:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿So they will not be able to make a bequest﴾, meaning: to give instructions (iṣāʾ). And His saying: ﴿nor will they return to their families﴾, meaning: they will not turn back (yanqalibūn). The meaning is that the Hour will not give them any respite at all.

Commentary of al-Sam'ani (Tafsir al-Quran) on surah 36, verse 51:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And the Horn is blown﴾. The first: it is the first blast (al-nafkha al-ula). The second: it is the other blast (al-nafkha al-ukhra). Between them is a period of forty years.

And His saying: ﴿And behold, they will rise from their graves to their Lord, hastening﴾, meaning: from the graves (al-qubur).

And His saying: ﴿to their Lord, hastening﴾, meaning: they will hurry. The poet said:

("Asalan" of the wolf, when he came near at the cool of the night, so he trotted (fanasal))

And Imru' al-Qays said:

(Slip off your garments from your garments, and go swiftly (tanaslu))

And al-naslan is above walking and below running.

Commentary of al-Sam'ani (Tafsir al-Quran) on surah 36, verse 52:

And His, the Exalted's, saying: ﴿They will say, "Woe to us! Who has raised us up from our resting place?"﴾ Ibn 'Abbas said: The punishment is lifted from them for the period between the two blasts (of the Trumpet). And on the authority of Ubayy ibn Ka'b, he said: They sleep a sleep before the Resurrection. And on the authority of Mujahid, he said: The punishment is lifted from them, so they doze and sleep.

And it is related on the authority of some scholars that this statement is made by the believers. The more apparent of the two opinions is the first, that it is the statement of the disbelievers. Ibn Mas'ud recited: "Who has roused us from our resting place" (man ahabana min marqadina).

And His saying: ﴿This is what the Most Merciful promised, and the messengers spoke the truth.﴾ is the statement of the believers, answering the disbelievers. According to the other opinion, it is the statement of the believers, and they answer it to themselves. And His saying: ﴿and the messengers spoke the truth﴾ is clear.
And His saying: ﴿It will be but a single blast, and behold, they will all be brought before Us﴾ — i.e., present (ḥāḍirūn).

Almost all of it is a Qur'anic quotation, so I'll render it as given. The sentence reads: "The saying of Allah, the Exalted: ﴿So on that Day no soul will be wronged in the least, and you will not be recompensed except for what you used to do﴾. The apparent meaning is clear."

Commentary of al-Sam'ani (Tafsir al-Quran) on surah 36, verse 55:

The words of the Most High: ﴿Indeed, the companions of the Garden today are busy in enjoyment.﴾ It is also recited as "fī shughl" (in busyness) with the vowel sukūn (jazm) on the lām. Ibn ʿAbbās said: "busy in deflowering the virgins." And from him also: he said, "busy in the striking of the lutes." The first is the one well known among the exegetes.

The third view: "busy away from the punishment of the people of the Fire."

And His words: ﴿fākihūn (enjoying fruits)﴾. It is also recited as "fakihūn" (merry, jesting). Some scholars said: the two have the same meaning, like al-ḥadhar and al-ḥādhir (wary). Others distinguished between them. They said: al-fakih is one who is pleased in himself and admires his own state, while al-fākih is one who possesses fruit. Jesting is also called fukāha. Al-Ḥuṭay'a said:

(And you called me, and claimed that you were the son of one who gives the guest dates and milk.)

meaning: one who possesses dates and one who possesses milk. Another said:

(Merry beside the food-spread whenever it is brought in, uprooting the firmly-set tent-pegs of the bedouin tents.)

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿They and their spouses are in shade﴾. "Ẓilāl" is the plural of "ẓill" (shade). His saying: ﴿on couches﴾: in the exegesis, these are couches of gold, adorned with pearls, chrysolite and rubies, upon which are canopies (ḥajāl).

Tha'lab said: "Al-arā'ik (couches) are not called arīka unless it is beneath a canopy (ḥajla)."

His saying: ﴿reclining﴾, meaning that they are people of reclining (ittikā'). The mention of reclining in Paradise is because they do not sleep.

Almost. Let me translate it now.

The Exalted's saying: ﴿For them therein is fruit, and for them is whatever they call for﴾. That is: whatever they wish for. The Arabs say: "Call for whatever you want," meaning: "Wish for whatever you want." Al-A'sha said:

(Wine, ... whatever he called for)

(An aged wine, whatever he called for ...)

Commentary of al-Sam'ani (Tafsir al-Quran) on surah 36, verse 58:

The words of the Exalted: ﴿Peace, a word from a Lord, Most Merciful.﴾ Most of the exegetes say that its meaning is: Allah greets them with peace (salam). And His words ﴿a word﴾ mean: He says a word.

In the narration of Jabir from the Prophet (ﷺ), he said: "While the people of Paradise are in their bliss, a light shines upon them and their Lord, may He be exalted and glorified, looks down upon them, and He greets them with peace..." and the report continues to its end. It is also said: the angels greet them with peace from their Lord. And it has been said: Allah grants them safety (salamah), and He says: "Attain the everlasting safety." And His words ﴿from a Lord, Most Merciful﴾ mean: Compassionate (ʿatuf).

"And [it will be said], 'Separate yourselves today, O criminals!'" That is, separate yourselves from the believers.

It is said in the tafsir: the Jews are one group, the Christians are a group, the Magians are a group, the Sabians are a group, the polytheists are a group, and the believers are a group. The meaning is that Allah the Exalted distinguishes between the people of righteousness and the people of corruption, between the polytheists and the believers, and between the hypocrites and the sincere.

Allah's words: ﴿Did I not charge you, O children of Adam, that you should not worship Satan?﴾ That is: did I not command you? ﴿Do not worship Satan﴾ means: do not obey Satan, and worshipping Satan is obeying him. And His words: ﴿Indeed, he is to you a clear enemy﴾ mean: an enemy who is evidently hostile.
And His saying: ﴿And that you worship Me; this is a straight path﴾ — i.e., a straight path upon the truth.

"The saying of Him, exalted is He: ﴿And he had already led astray a great multitude from among you﴾. It is read also as "jibillan kathiran" (a great multitude), and it is read as "jibalan" with the jim and the ba' pronounced with damma. Its meaning is: a large creation. Al-Dahhak said: ten thousand or more. And it is reported from some of them: a large creation whose number none can count except Allah. His saying: ﴿Did you not then understand?﴾ means: did you not then reason regarding My signs, and reflect upon them with the reflection of one who understands,"

This is the wording of the passage. Translating:

On His saying, the Exalted: ﴿This is Hell which you were promised﴾, meaning: which you were promised entry into because of your disbelief.

Commentary of al-Sam'ani (Tafsir al-Quran) on surah 36, verse 64:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Burn therein today﴾, meaning: enter it and endure its heat. [﴿for what you used to disbelieve﴾],

Commentary of al-Sam'ani (Tafsir al-Quran) on surah 36, verse 65:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Today We shall seal their mouths﴾. The people of tafsir (exegesis) said: This is when the disbelievers deny their disbelief and their rejection of God's messengers, so God seals their mouths and permits the limbs to bear witness to what they did.

In the well-known reports it is related that the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "A servant will say on the Day of Resurrection: 'O Lord, I will not permit against myself except a witness from myself.' So God will seal his mouth, and say to his limbs: 'Speak!' The limbs will speak of what he did. Then He will leave him free with his tongue, and he will say to his limbs: 'Away with you, destruction! It was for you that I was contending.'"

And in another report, also from the Prophet (ﷺ), he said: "People will be brought on the Day of Resurrection with their mouths fitted with a fidam (a stopper), and their limbs will bear witness to what they did. The first to bear witness will be a person's thigh and his palm."

As for His saying: ﴿And their hands will speak to Us, and their feet will bear witness to what they used to earn﴾, we have already explained it.

Some people have denied that the limbs speak, saying: the meaning of "speaking" is that there exists a sign indicating that they did what they did. But the correct view is that they truly speak, and the speech of the limbs is not far-fetched for the power of God, exalted is He.

Commentary of al-Sam'ani (Tafsir al-Quran) on surah 36, verse 66:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And if We willed, We would have obliterated their eyes﴾ meaning: We would have blinded them. It is also said: We would have led them astray from guidance. Al-Mubarrad and Thaʻlab said: "al-matmus" and "al-tamis" are the one who has no slit in his eyes.

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿So they would race to the path﴾ meaning: they would hasten to the way. And His saying: ﴿So how would they see?﴾ its meaning is: from where would they see? It is also said: how then would they see?

"The saying of Allah, the Exalted: ﴿And if We willed, We would have transformed them in their places﴾, meaning: We would have made them apes and swine in their dwellings. And it is said: We would have made them sit down on their feet. And His saying: ﴿So they would not be able to proceed﴾, meaning: going forth. And His saying: ﴿nor could they return﴾, meaning: they would not return to their families."

Commentary of al-Sam'ani (Tafsir al-Quran) on surah 36, verse 68:

The words of the Most High: ﴿And whoever We grant long life, We reverse him in creation.﴾ It is also read: "nunakkisuhu fi al-khalq" (ننكسه فِي الْخلق). That is: whoever We prolong his life, We reverse him in creation, meaning: We return him to the lowest stage of life (arhal al-'umr, أرذل الْعُمر). It is said: the reversal in creation is the weakening of the limbs after their strength. And His words: ﴿Will they not then understand?﴾ their meaning: will they not understand My signs?

Commentary of al-Sam'ani (Tafsir al-Quran) on surah 36, verse 69:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And We did not teach him poetry, nor is it befitting for him﴾. They said: The polytheists used to claim that Muhammad was a poet and that the Qur'an was poetry. So God, exalted is He, sent down this verse: ﴿And We did not teach him poetry, nor is it befitting for him﴾, meaning: poetry does not come easily to him, nor does it fall into metre for him. And in a report: "The Prophet recited one day:

(Islam and white hair are enough as a deterrent for a man...)

Abu Bakr said: 'May my father and mother be your ransom, O Messenger of God, it is: (White hair and Islam are enough as a deterrent for a man...)'

The Prophet said: 'Both are one.' Abu Bakr said: 'I bear witness that you do not speak poetry, nor is it befitting for you.'"

And on the authority of ʿĀʾisha, may God be pleased with her, that the Prophet recited a verse of Ṭarafa:

(Days will reveal to you what you did not know, and there will come to you with news one who has not provided for you...)

The Prophet said: "There will come to you with news one who has not provided for you."

And His saying: ﴿It is nothing but a reminder and a clear Qur'an﴾, meaning: a admonition and a plain Qur'an.

"His saying, the Exalted: ﴿That he may warn whoever is alive﴾, i.e., rational (ʿāqil). It was also said: a believer. Qatādah said: one whose heart is alive. And His saying: ﴿and the word may be justified against the disbelievers﴾, i.e., the proof of the punishment becomes binding upon the disbelievers."

The Exalted said: ﴿Have they not seen that We created for them, of what Our hands have done, cattle, and they are their owners?﴾ That is: of what We Ourselves undertook to create and originate. Regarding the "hands," the preferable position is to affirm them without interpreting them.

And His saying: ﴿and they are their owners﴾ means: those who control them (ḍābiṭūn). Sībawayh recited:

"You are not among the handsome of mankind, nor do I control the camel's head when it bolts"

That is: I control (aḍbiṭ).

His words, may He be exalted: ﴿And We have made them subservient to them﴾, meaning: We made them docile for them. And His words: ﴿so some of them they ride﴾, "ar-rukub" (the mounts) is that which is ridden. And His words: ﴿and from them they eat﴾, the meaning is apparent.

Almighty Allah says: ﴿And for them therein are benefits and drinks. Will they not then be grateful?﴾ That is, in the cattle there are benefits from their wool, their fur and their hair. As for His words ﴿and drinks﴾, that is, from their milk. As for His words ﴿Will they not then be grateful?﴾, He means: for these blessings.
Allah's saying: ﴿And they took gods besides Allah, hoping that they might be helped﴾, i.e., that they would ward off the punishment from them.

Commentary of al-Sam'ani (Tafsir al-Quran) on surah 36, verse 75:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿They are not able to help them﴾, meaning: the idols are not able to ward off the punishment from them.

And His saying: ﴿And they are an army brought before them﴾ has two interpretations. One of them: "And they are an army for them", meaning: the disbelievers are an army and followers for the idols.

The second view: this refers to the Resurrection, namely that every worshipped thing that was worshipped besides Allah will be called, and it will be brought along with its followers, and those who worshipped it are as though they were its army. His saying: ﴿Then they are brought forth (muhdarun)﴾ means they will be brought before the Fire, and its meaning is: they will be made to enter it.

"His saying: ﴿So let not their word grieve you﴾, meaning: their word about you, that he is a sorcerer, or a liar, or a poet.

And His saying: ﴿Indeed We know﴾ — this is the beginning of a statement. His saying: ﴿what they conceal﴾ means: of denial (al-takdhib). And His saying: ﴿and what they reveal﴾ means: of the worship of idols."

Commentary of al-Sam'ani (Tafsir al-Quran) on surah 36, verse 77:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Has not man seen that We created him from a drop of semen, and then behold, he is an open adversary?﴾ The verse was revealed concerning Ubayy ibn Khalaf, for it is related that he took a decayed bone and crumbled it between his fingers, and said: "O Muhammad, do you claim that this will be brought to life and resurrected?"

In some exegeses it is mentioned that the one who said this was al-'As ibn Wa'il al-Sahmi, but the first (view) is more well-known. So the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Yes, and Allah, may He be exalted, will cause you to die, then resurrect you, then cause you to enter the Fire of Hell."

As for His saying, ﴿then behold, he is an open adversary﴾, it means: one who disputes with extreme vehemence. As for the argument against them in the creation of man from a drop of semen, it is that re-creation is easier, in what people understand, than the initial creation.

Commentary of al-Sam'ani (Tafsir al-Quran) on surah 36, verse 78:

The words of the Most High: ﴿And he has struck for Us an example and forgotten his own creation﴾. "Striking an example" (ḍarb al-mathal) is what We have explained in His saying. And His saying: ﴿and forgotten his own creation﴾ means: and he neglected to reflect upon the origin of His creation.

And His saying: ﴿He said, "Who will give life to the bones when they are decayed?"﴾ Ramm (decayed) refers to the bones that have crumbled away.

Commentary of al-Sam'ani (Tafsir al-Quran) on surah 36, verse 79:

His words, exalted is He: ﴿Say: He who brought them into being the first time will give them life again, and He is Knowing of every creation.﴾ That is: Knowing (ʿalim).

Commentary of al-Sam'ani (Tafsir al-Quran) on surah 36, verses 80–83:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Who has made for you fire from the green tree﴾. The people of tafsir said: what is meant by it is the markh and the 'affar, two pieces of wood from which the Arabs strike fire (tawriya), just as people strike fire from iron and stone. His saying "yuwri" means: yaqdah (strikes sparks). The Arabs say: "In every tree there is fire, and the markh and the 'affar have the most glory." And from Abu Salih, he said: "In trees there is fire, except the tree of the 'affar."

His saying: ﴿then, behold, you kindle from it﴾, i.e., you strike (sparks) and kindle (fire).

His saying: ﴿Is not He who created the heavens and the earth able to create the like of them?﴾ i.e., to bring into being creatures like them. It was also said: to restore them on the Day of Resurrection, so that they become creatures as they were.

His saying: ﴿Yes, and He is the All-Creating, the All-Knowing﴾. Its meaning: say, "Yes," and it is an address to the Messenger. We have already explained the difference between bala (yes, in answer to a negative) and na'am (yes) earlier, and in answer to a negative question it is not correct except with the word bala. It was also said: God, the Exalted, said, answering Himself: "Yes, and He is the All-Creating, the All-Knowing." The Khallaq is the One who creates again and again, and the 'Alim is the One who knows His creation.

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿His command, when He intends a thing, is only that He says to it, "Be," and it is.﴾ We have explained this before. His saying: ﴿So glory be to the One in whose hand is the dominion of all things﴾, i.e., the sovereignty of all things.

His saying: ﴿And to Him you will be returned﴾, i.e., you will be brought back on the Day of Resurrection.

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Who has made for you fire from the green tree﴾. The people of tafsir said: what is meant by it is the markh and the 'affar, two pieces of wood from which the Arabs strike fire (tawriya), just as people strike fire from iron and stone. And from Abu Salih, he said: "In trees there is fire, except the tree of the 'affar."
